narrative_md:
**Announcing HS2's northern cancellation at his own party conference in Manchester, Sunak promised £36 billion of savings for regional transport. Within a year the IfG said the savings number was overstated and the replacement schemes were underfunded.**

On 4 October 2023 Rishi Sunak used his Conservative Party conference speech in Manchester to cancel HS2 Phase 2 — the Birmingham-to-Manchester leg — and redirect a claimed £36bn into 'Network North'. The fiscal arithmetic was disputed immediately. Eighteen months later the replacement programme is partial, the High Speed line ends in West London at Old Oak Common, and Manchester still has no committed high-speed rail link.

**The cancellation.** HS2 had been approved in stages: Phase 1 (London Euston to Birmingham) from 2012, Phase 2a (Birmingham to Crewe) from 2017, Phase 2b (Crewe to Manchester, and the eastern leg via East Midlands to Leeds) progressively scaled back from 2021. The NAO's 2023 review projected whole-scheme costs of £58-67bn for Phases 1 and 2a alone. Sunak's October 2023 decision cancelled Phase 2b Western Leg (Crewe-Manchester) and 2a (Birmingham-Crewe), leaving only Phase 1 — and even that stopped short of Euston, terminating at Old Oak Common pending private-sector funding for the central London extension.

**The £36bn 'saved'.** The Government claimed £36bn of savings vs original Phase 2b/2a full-scheme cost. The IfG, Bridget Rosewell's independent review, and Greengauge 21 all pointed out that: (a) a substantial share of the £36bn was uncosted contingency; (b) sunk costs already spent on Phase 2 land acquisition, design and enabling works (around £2bn) would need to be written off; (c) the Network North replacement programme included projects already funded under City Region Sustainable Transport Settlements, so some 'new' money wasn't new. Net genuine saving, per IfG's October 2024 update, closer to £10-15bn.

**Network North.** The replacement package announced on 4 October 2023 covered: a new Northern Powerhouse Rail scheme (Liverpool-Manchester-Leeds-Sheffield, largely on upgraded existing track), Midlands Rail Hub, £8.3bn for local road resurfacing (the 'pothole fund'), £4.7bn for bus services, Devon Great Western electrification, and Ely-Haughley junction upgrade. Few of these schemes have FBCs approved. Network North was not put in legislation; it was not ring-fenced.

**Labour's July 2024 position.** Louise Haigh as Transport Secretary retained the Network North branding initially, while commissioning the 2024 Rail Review. Her December 2024 statement confirmed Old Oak Common as the Phase 1 London terminus pending private-finance review for Euston — a position that has now held for 18 months. Manchester will be reached by upgraded conventional rail, not high-speed. NPR's precise route, procurement model and timeline remain uncommitted.

**The cost envelope for what remains.** HS2 Phase 1 — London (Old Oak Common) to Birmingham Curzon Street, plus a spur to Handsacre connecting to the existing West Coast Main Line — is still projected at £55-66bn in 2024-25 terms. The Public Accounts Committee described the programme as having 'lost its way'. Opening is now scheduled between 2029 and 2033, with Euston unresolved. Per-kilometre build cost is several times typical European high-speed rail norms.

**The wider lesson.** Large UK infrastructure projects have exhibited a consistent pattern: a strategic rationale (HS2 was about capacity on the West Coast Main Line, not just speed), optimism bias in costing, political appetite for phased announcements that lock future decisions, and late-stage retreat. The National Infrastructure Commission has argued the remedy is longer-term budgeted envelopes, like Germany's Bundesverkehrswegeplan — a single multi-decade investment plan with political buy-in across parties. Whether Labour's 2025 Infrastructure Strategy delivers that is the next test.
